title: A Python client for a stock game

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: What if you could run a stock-trading game from a Python script, with no real money at stake? That's what Antoine's small package, marketwatch, lets you do.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: A stock game? Like paper trading?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Exactly. MarketWatch runs a virtual stock game, and Antoine wanted to automate the chores in it. So he published a client on PyPI. Install it with pip, log in with your username and password, and you can list your games, check a price like Apple's, and more.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: It covers watchlists, where you create, list and update symbols. It reads games and their settings. It shows your portfolio, with positions and pending orders. It places buys and sells inside the game's rules. And it can fetch the leaderboard for a game.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Why not just poke the site with curl?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Because the game uses session cookies, game rules and leaderboards that change with the semester. A thin Python wrapper handles that in one place. Think of it as a remote control for the site: one login, then many buttons.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: And the design is intentionally small.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Right. It's a class-based client, so one login serves many calls in a script. Each endpoint gets its own explicit method, which makes the code easy to search. There's no database layer and no strategy engine, just HTTP shaped like the site. Strategies belong in your own repo.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Why did he want it documented?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: So teammates have a clear surface: here's how you list games, instead of passing around a script that breaks. The docs live on GitHub Pages, with the login details covered.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Where does it fit with his other work?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: It pairs naturally with his backtesting projects. BatchBacktesting runs strategies on historical data, and this client lets you try ideas inside a live game, handy for small bots and screening.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So the takeaway is a tidy wrapper that turns a game into something scriptable.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: That's it. The write-up has the links to PyPI, the docs and the source on GitHub.
